properties.Name: True Reformer Hall
properties.WhyShort: Home of the Savings Bank of the Great Fountain United Order of the True Reformers Bank and The Reformer newspaper.
properties.WhyLong: The Grand Fountain of the United Order of True Reformers was an African American fraternal organization that became the largest and most successful black business enterprise between 1881 and 1910. When William Washington Browne arrived in Richmond in December 1880, he was invited by local leaders to revive Virginia’s declining branch of True Reformers. On January 11, 1881, he announced plans to transform the order into a mutual benefit association focused on securing the financial future of its members at a time when no mainstream institutions would serve Black Americans. His broader vision was to build an entirely self-sufficient African American economy. The order provided members with death benefits, sick pay, and eventually a youth division teaching children thrift, self-reliance, and business skills. Between 1883 and 1885 the order saw the beginning of major growth, going from nine to fifty-two fountains.

properties.Name: Clay Street Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church
properties.WhyShort: The church stands as a reminder of the neighborhood's rich religious and architectural history.
properties.WhyLong: Constructed around 1850 and designed by prominent Richmond architect Albert West, Clay Street AME Church was originally built in the Italianate style. Around 1890, the building was updated with a Gothic Revival façade, reflecting changing architectural tastes of the period. Although the loss of its steeple and other alterations have changed its appearance, the church remains an important landmark in Jackson Ward. Today known as Hood Temple, it stands as a reminder of the neighborhood’s rich religious and architectural history.

properties.Name: Shockoe Hill Cemetery/African Burying Ground
properties.WhyShort: Segregated Cemetery which restricted African americans to the potter field to later be subjugated to grave robbing by med school and built over by 64.
properties.WhyLong: The Shockoe Hill African Burying Ground opened in 1816 as the city's second burial ground for Black Richmonders — one acre designated for free people of color, one for enslaved people. Located near the poorhouse at the terminus of Fifth Street, it was administered as the segregated counterpart to the walled Shockoe Hill Cemetery. By the 1840s the site was badly overcrowded, with one official counting fifty burials in a single month. The grounds were prey to graverobbers serving Richmond's medical schools for decades, a practice authorities largely ignored. By 1879, after an estimated 22,000 burials, the city halted interments and began repurposing the site — regrading streets, extending roads, and using exposed remains as fill.

properties.Name: A.D. Price Funeral Home
properties.WhyShort: Historic funeral home that played an important role to many Black families over time.
properties.WhyLong: Alfred Douglas Price was born in 1860 in Hanover County and came to Richmond where he trained as a blacksmith and wheelwright before entering the funeral and livery business. In the early 1880s he established the A.D. Price Funeral Home at 212 E. Leigh Street — his first business in Jackson Ward. It grew to become one of the largest African American-owned funeral establishments in the country, a testament to the entrepreneurial spirit that defined Jackson Ward in this era. The building at 212 E. Leigh Street is today a private apartment building.

properties.Name: Bill "Bojangles" Robinson Home/Birth Place
properties.WhyShort: Home of famous entertainer known for his tap dancing and "stair dance."
properties.WhyLong: Born in 1878 on Third Street, Bill “Bojangles” Robinson was an entertainer best known for his tap dancing. In 1918 he introduced his “stair dance” in which he tapped up and down a staircase. Through pure talent, he was able to break down barriers set by segregation allowing him to perform on Broadway and Hollywood. Robinson was also a philanthropist, donating large sums to Black charities in Harlem. In 1931, Robinson saw Black children attempting to cross a dangerous intersection in order to get to school. He paid all the costs to get the first traffic light “North of Broad” put up at this intersection.

properties.Name: Van de Vyver/Saint Joseph Catholic Church
properties.WhyShort: Serving as home to both Van de Vyver Catholic School and Saint Joseph Catholic Church, this building hosted one of the largest public institutions for Black students and the first Catholic congregation organized for African Americans in Virginia
properties.WhyLong: Van de Vyver Catholic School was founded by Bishop Keane in 1887 and became a cornerstone of Black education in Richmond. Offering kindergarten through high school education, school filled the educational gap created by the segregated school system in Richmond. Over time Van de Vyver became one of the largest private schools for Black students in Richmond offering a curriculum that included auto mechanics, dressmaking, tailoring, reading, writing, and arithmetic. Along with the school, the building was also used by a church. Saint Joseph Catholic Church was established in this building, creating the first Catholic congregation organized for African Americans in Virginia.
